Esquema vacinal

Desde 2024, o Brasil adotou o esquema vacinal contra o HPV em dose única para crianças e adolescentes de 9 a 14 anos, substituindo o modelo anterior de duas doses. A iniciativa faz parte do compromisso do Brasil com a OMS para eliminar o câncer de colo do útero, que prevê atingir 90% de cobertura vacinal entre meninas até 2030.

O país foi além da meta ao incluir também os meninos e, em 2024, passou a adotar a dose única da vacina contra o HPV, em linha com recomendações internacionais.

Desde 2014, o Sistema Único de Saúde (SUS) já distribuiu mais de 75 milhões de doses, consolidando uma das políticas de vacinação mais abrangentes do mundo. O programa inclui meninos, imunossuprimidos, vítimas de violência sexual, usuários de PrEP e crianças com papilomatose respiratória recorrente.

Para pessoas imunocomprometidas, como aquelas vivendo com HIV/AIDS, pacientes oncológicos e transplantados, o esquema permanece em três doses, independentemente da idade. Além disso, pessoas vítimas de violência sexual e usuários de PrEP entre 15 e 45 anos devem receber três doses da vacina, enquanto crianças e adolescentes de 9 a 14 anos vítimas de violência sexual continuam com duas doses.

The proportions of participants not in a relationship and with multiple sexual partners in the last year increased significantly among both men and women. Among men, the proportions of individuals who initiated sexual activity after age 15 increased from 59.9% (55.0–64.7) to 66.3% (62.7–69.7). No differences were observed in alcohol consumption or reported condom use at last intercourse. In POP-Brazil 2, there were 116 men (3.6%) and 32 women (0.6%) living with HIV, of whom 44 men and 12 women had received HPV vaccination. There were no differences in the HIV prevalence among the two surveys. Vaccination coverage in POP-Brazil 2 was significantly lower among men (31.1%; 27.4–35.0) compared to women (61.8%; 60.1–63.5) (Table 1). It is important to consider that POP2 participants (aged 16–25 years, birth cohorts 1995–2007) faced substantially different vaccination opportunities due to changes in the HPV vaccination policies through time (Supplementary Fig. 1)<sup>6</sup>. Older participants depended more on private access, and many had already exceeded the recommended age range by 2014, making vaccination less likely, particularly among boys. The weighted mean time since vaccination was 8 years (7.8–8.1) among women and 6.5 years (5.7–7.2) among men.

In Brazil, the quadrivalent vaccine was introduced in the public immunization program as a two-dose schedule in 2014, initially targeting girls aged 11–13 years. A year later, the program was expanded to include younger girls, lowering the minimum age to nine years. In 2017, it was further extended to older girls, raising the maximum age to 14 years and also including boys (aged 11–14 years) and high-risk adult populations, such as people living with HIV, oncology patients, and those who had undergone solid organ or bone marrow transplants<sup>6</sup>. Since 2024, the vaccination schedule has been updated to a single dose for boys and girls aged 9–14 years, and for the catch-up of unvaccinated adolescents of both sexes aged 15–19 years in 2025. The HPV vaccination was also expanded to pre-exposure prophylaxis users, victims of sexual violence, individuals with recurrent respiratory papillomatosis<sup>6</sup>. Considering the first dose, the vaccination coverage in Brazil was estimated at 83.21% among women and 67.57% among men aged 9–14 years in 2024<sup>7</sup>.

Just three years after the vaccine’s introduction in Brazil, our previous findings showed that vaccinated girls had significantly lower prevalence of genotypes covered by the 4vHPV vaccine compared to unvaccinated ones<sup>8</sup>. However, a decade after the implementation of the quadrivalent HPV vaccine in Brazil, the real population-level impact on HPV prevalence remains largely unknown when comparing pre- and post-vaccine eras. While several studies have demonstrated positive vaccine impact in HPV prevalence, they primarily focus on high-income countries, with limited data from Latin America, a region with extensive vaccination programs and high cervical cancer incidence<sup>9,10</sup>. Therefore, we aimed to evaluate the population-level impact of HPV vaccination on HPV prevalence among Brazilians aged 16–25.

## Discussion

This was the largest study to assess the impact of the quadrivalent HPV vaccine in Latin America. There was a clear decline in the prevalence of HPV types covered by the 4vHPV vaccine among young people. A decline was observed not only among vaccinated individuals but also at the population level, including unvaccinated women. These findings indicate that the national HPV immunization program effectively prevents the spread of oncogenic HPV genotypes included in the quadrivalent vaccine among sexually active women and men after the introduction of the vaccine in Brazil in 2014. Vaccine coverage plays a pivotal role in controlling HPV transmission. The reduction in HPV prevalence was more pronounced in age groups with higher vaccine coverage, as demonstrated by the age-stratified analysis. There was no difference in HPV prevalence according to the number of doses of vaccine.

Findings from POP-Brazil had already demonstrated the vaccine’s effectiveness in Brazil, with prevalence of HPV types 6, 11, 16, and 18 declining by 56.8% (from 15.64% in unvaccinated women to 6.76% in vaccinated women)<sup>8</sup>. As a repeated cross-sectional survey, POP-Brazil 2 demonstrated substantial vaccine impact: between the surveys, multivariate analysis showed that vaccination led to an 81% reduction in the vaccine-targeted genotypes among vaccinated women and a 61% reduction among vaccinated men. Notably, younger women showed a greater reduction in the prevalence of HPV genotypes covered by the 4vHPV vaccine compared to older women.

## Methods

### Study design/population

We used data from repeated cross-sectional surveys to compare genital HPV prevalence among sexually active 16- to 25-year-old men and women between pre- and post-vaccine eras in Brazil. The first study (POP-Brazil 1) was conducted between 2016 and 2017, in the 26 state capitals and the Federal District of Brazil, right after the introduction of the HPV vaccination program. The second study (POP-Brazil 2), was conducted between 2020 and 2023 with the same population target. Participants who had not initiated sexual activity, pregnant women, women who had given birth within the previous six months, women who had undergone a hysterectomy or trachelectomy, and women who had ever had grade 2 or higher cervical intraepithelial neoplasia were not included. Both phases of the POP-Brazil survey were conducted according to the original study protocol<sup>11</sup>, ensuring consistent methodological characteristics and data collection procedures that enabled data comparison across the two time periods.

Participants were recruited from public health units and responded to a structured questionnaire conducted by health professionals who received rigorous training and onsite certification. Vaccination status was assessed as a dichotomous variable (vaccinated/unvaccinated). Participants were classified as vaccinated against HPV if they self-reported vaccination or had documented vaccination history (verified at the time of participation or through medical records and vaccination registries), regardless of dose number and vaccine type. Time since vaccination (years) was calculated by subtracting self-reported age at vaccination from age at interview. Sociodemographic variables included age, self-reported skin color/ethnicity, and socioeconomic status, which was computed based on a score of self-reported number of household goods according with the Associação Brasileira de Empresas de Pesquisa (ABEP). We also explored alcohol consumption in the last year, partnership status, condom use during the last sexual intercourse, number of sexual partners in the last year, and the age of sexual debut. Because retesting for HIV is not recommended for individuals who are already confirmed to be HIV-positive, we first assessed HIV status. For those that are HIV negative, unsure, or never have been tested, an HIV test was offered, with the result being incorporated in the HIV status determination.

O país foi além da meta ao incluir também os meninos e, em 2024, passou a adotar a dose única da vacina contra o HPV, em linha com recomendações internacionais.

Desde 2014, o Sistema Único de Saúde (SUS) já distribuiu mais de 75 milhões de doses, consolidando uma das políticas de vacinação mais abrangentes do mundo. O programa inclui meninos, imunossuprimidos, vítimas de violência sexual, usuários de PrEP e crianças com papilomatose respiratória recorrente.

Para pessoas imunocomprometidas, como aquelas vivendo com HIV/AIDS, pacientes oncológicos e transplantados, o esquema permanece em três doses, independentemente da idade. Além disso, pessoas vítimas de violência sexual e usuários de PrEP entre 15 e 45 anos devem receber três doses da vacina, enquanto crianças e adolescentes de 9 a 14 anos vítimas de violência sexual continuam com duas doses.

In Brazil, the quadrivalent vaccine was introduced in the public immunization program as a two-dose schedule in 2014, initially targeting girls aged 11–13 years. A year later, the program was expanded to include younger girls, lowering the minimum age to nine years. In 2017, it was further extended to older girls, raising the maximum age to 14 years and also including boys (aged 11–14 years) and high-risk adult populations, such as people living with HIV, oncology patients, and those who had undergone solid organ or bone marrow transplants<sup>6</sup>. Since 2024, the vaccination schedule has been updated to a single dose for boys and girls aged 9–14 years, and for the catch-up of unvaccinated adolescents of both sexes aged 15–19 years in 2025. The HPV vaccination was also expanded to pre-exposure prophylaxis users, victims of sexual violence, individuals with recurrent respiratory papillomatosis<sup>6</sup>. Considering the first dose, the vaccination coverage in Brazil was estimated at 83.21% among women and 67.57% among men aged 9–14 years in 2024<sup>7</sup>.

Just three years after the vaccine’s introduction in Brazil, our previous findings showed that vaccinated girls had significantly lower prevalence of genotypes covered by the 4vHPV vaccine compared to unvaccinated ones<sup>8</sup>. However, a decade after the implementation of the quadrivalent HPV vaccine in Brazil, the real population-level impact on HPV prevalence remains largely unknown when comparing pre- and post-vaccine eras. While several studies have demonstrated positive vaccine impact in HPV prevalence, they primarily focus on high-income countries, with limited data from Latin America, a region with extensive vaccination programs and high cervical cancer incidence<sup>9,10</sup>. Therefore, we aimed to evaluate the population-level impact of HPV vaccination on HPV prevalence among Brazilians aged 16–25.

## Discussion

This was the largest study to assess the impact of the quadrivalent HPV vaccine in Latin America. There was a clear decline in the prevalence of HPV types covered by the 4vHPV vaccine among young people. A decline was observed not only among vaccinated individuals but also at the population level, including unvaccinated women. These findings indicate that the national HPV immunization program effectively prevents the spread of oncogenic HPV genotypes included in the quadrivalent vaccine among sexually active women and men after the introduction of the vaccine in Brazil in 2014. Vaccine coverage plays a pivotal role in controlling HPV transmission. The reduction in HPV prevalence was more pronounced in age groups with higher vaccine coverage, as demonstrated by the age-stratified analysis. There was no difference in HPV prevalence according to the number of doses of vaccine.

Findings from POP-Brazil had already demonstrated the vaccine’s effectiveness in Brazil, with prevalence of HPV types 6, 11, 16, and 18 declining by 56.8% (from 15.64% in unvaccinated women to 6.76% in vaccinated women)<sup>8</sup>. As a repeated cross-sectional survey, POP-Brazil 2 demonstrated substantial vaccine impact: between the surveys, multivariate analysis showed that vaccination led to an 81% reduction in the vaccine-targeted genotypes among vaccinated women and a 61% reduction among vaccinated men. Notably, younger women showed a greater reduction in the prevalence of HPV genotypes covered by the 4vHPV vaccine compared to older women.

## Methods

### Study design/population

We used data from repeated cross-sectional surveys to compare genital HPV prevalence among sexually active 16- to 25-year-old men and women between pre- and post-vaccine eras in Brazil. The first study (POP-Brazil 1) was conducted between 2016 and 2017, in the 26 state capitals and the Federal District of Brazil, right after the introduction of the HPV vaccination program. The second study (POP-Brazil 2), was conducted between 2020 and 2023 with the same population target. Participants who had not initiated sexual activity, pregnant women, women who had given birth within the previous six months, women who had undergone a hysterectomy or trachelectomy, and women who had ever had grade 2 or higher cervical intraepithelial neoplasia were not included. Both phases of the POP-Brazil survey were conducted according to the original study protocol<sup>11</sup>, ensuring consistent methodological characteristics and data collection procedures that enabled data comparison across the two time periods.

Participants were recruited from public health units and responded to a structured questionnaire conducted by health professionals who received rigorous training and onsite certification. Vaccination status was assessed as a dichotomous variable (vaccinated/unvaccinated). Participants were classified as vaccinated against HPV if they self-reported vaccination or had documented vaccination history (verified at the time of participation or through medical records and vaccination registries), regardless of dose number and vaccine type. Time since vaccination (years) was calculated by subtracting self-reported age at vaccination from age at interview. Sociodemographic variables included age, self-reported skin color/ethnicity, and socioeconomic status, which was computed based on a score of self-reported number of household goods according with the Associação Brasileira de Empresas de Pesquisa (ABEP). We also explored alcohol consumption in the last year, partnership status, condom use during the last sexual intercourse, number of sexual partners in the last year, and the age of sexual debut. Because retesting for HIV is not recommended for individuals who are already confirmed to be HIV-positive, we first assessed HIV status. For those that are HIV negative, unsure, or never have been tested, an HIV test was offered, with the result being incorporated in the HIV status determination.
